name: Face pulls / band pull-aparts

lead: Face pulls and band pull-aparts are accessory exercises for the back of the shoulders and the upper back. They are done with a cable and rope or a simple resistance band.
People add them to training to pull the shoulders back, build rounder rear delts and stand more upright, which they say gives a wider, more athletic shoulder line.

paras: The movements load the rear deltoids, the muscles between the shoulder blades and the outward-rotating rotator-cuff muscles, which balance the chest and front-shoulder work from pressing exercises.
Loads are light and the exercises are generally regarded as low-risk; guidance usually stresses controlled form, and people with shoulder pain are advised to seek individual advice.

angle.text: Face pulls and band pull-aparts build the rear delts and upper-back muscles that hold the shoulders back. People use them alongside pressing work to balance the front of the shoulder and to stand and look more upright, with rounder shoulders from behind and the side.

lead: Face pulls and band pull-aparts are upper-back exercises that train the rear deltoids, the muscles between the shoulder blades and the small rotator-cuff muscles that turn the arm outward. A face pull is usually done with a rope attachment on a cable stack set near head height, pulling toward the face with the elbows high. A band pull-aparts is done by holding a resistance band at arm's length in front of the chest and drawing the hands apart until the band touches the chest.

People in lifting and looksmaxxing circles use them to improve posture and shoulder shape. Stronger rear delts and mid-back muscles are said to pull the shoulders back, open the chest and give the shoulders a rounder, fuller look from the side and behind, which proponents say helps a V-taper and a more upright, taller-looking stance.

Both movements are light, low-load exercises that are commonly added to the end of pressing-heavy training days. They are popular partly because they need little equipment: a band is cheap and portable, and the cable version is found in most gyms.

paras: The face pull is performed at a cable station with a rope handle at roughly face height. The lifter pulls the rope toward the forehead or nose while spreading the hands apart and rotating the upper arms outward, finishing with the elbows high and the shoulder blades squeezed together. Variants use a band anchored to a rack or door instead of a cable.

The band pull-apart uses a loop or tube band held in both hands at shoulder height with straight arms. The hands move outward to the sides until the band reaches the chest, then return slowly. Bands of different thickness change how hard the movement is, and the exercise can be done with light bands for many repetitions.

Both exercises load the posterior shoulder: the rear deltoid, the rhomboids and middle trapezius that draw the shoulder blades together, and the infraspinatus and teres minor that rotate the arm outward. Coaches commonly describe these as the counterpart to the chest and front-shoulder muscles trained by bench and overhead presses.

Because the loads are light and the movement is repeated for higher repetitions, practitioners often treat the work as a way to build muscle in an area that heavy rows do not always reach, and as a low-fatigue addition that can be done frequently.

In appearance-focused communities the exercises are discussed under posture, shoulder width and the V-taper. Proponents say that well-developed rear delts add visible roundness and width to the shoulders when viewed from behind and at an angle, and that a stronger upper back makes it easier to stand with the shoulders back and the chest open.

Some users pair them with stretching of the chest and front shoulders as part of routines aimed at reducing a rounded-shoulder or forward-head posture, which they associate with looking shorter and less athletic. Posture routines commonly list face pulls, band pull-aparts, rows and similar movements together.

Because loads are light, the exercises are generally regarded as low-risk. Coaching guidance typically emphasises controlled movement, keeping the neck relaxed and avoiding leaning back to use momentum. People with shoulder pain or injury are commonly advised to check technique with a coach or clinician.
